paragraphs.text: For most of history, sleep was regarded as a passive state, a period in which the body and brain simply rested. Since the middle of the twentieth century, however, scientists have shown that the sleeping brain is remarkably active, and that one of its most important tasks is the processing of memories formed during the day.

Sleep is not a single, uniform state. Over the course of a night, the brain passes through a cycle of stages roughly every ninety minutes. In deep, or slow-wave, sleep, which dominates the first half of the night, electrical activity in the brain slows down and becomes highly synchronised. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, during which most vivid dreams occur, becomes longer and more frequent towards the morning. Each of these stages appears to contribute to memory in a different way.

Deep sleep seems to be particularly important for memories of facts and events. During this stage, the hippocampus, a region of the brain that stores new information temporarily, repeatedly 'replays' recent experiences. Recordings from rats that had learned to run through a maze showed the same patterns of brain activity during sleep as during the task itself, but at a speed several times faster. Researchers believe this replay helps transfer information to the cortex, where it can be stored for the long term.

REM sleep, by contrast, has been linked to creativity and problem-solving. In a well-known experiment at the University of Lübeck in Germany, volunteers were given a mathematical task that could be solved much faster by using a hidden rule. Those who slept for eight hours before returning to the task were more than twice as likely to discover the rule as those who had stayed awake for the same length of time. The researchers suggested that sleep had allowed the brain to reorganise the information and notice a pattern that had not been obvious.

The implications for students are clear. Studying late into the night before an exam may reduce the amount of sleep, and therefore the amount of memory processing, that takes place. One study of university students found that those who slept less than six hours a night achieved lower grades than those who slept more, even after differences in study time had been taken into account. Short daytime naps may also help: in several experiments, a nap of sixty to ninety minutes improved performance on memory tests almost as much as a full night's sleep.

Teenagers face a particular difficulty. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts so that young people naturally feel sleepy later in the evening and wake later in the morning. Early school start times therefore force many teenagers to get up before their brains are ready. When a number of schools in the United States moved their start times from around 7.30 to 8.30 am, students slept on average forty-five minutes longer, and attendance and grades improved. Despite such findings, most schools have been reluctant to change, often because of the cost of reorganising transport.
